A.notes: Senior-level and technically sound, but the longest and least concise of the three. Presents two full approaches plus a dedicated 'why to avoid the other options' table and a separate recommendation section — enumerates rather than committing tightly. Well over the input length; violates the conciseness preference most.

B.notes: Most opinionated and focused: leads with one clear recommendation (Redis dirty-flag), addresses the 2000 TPS / EDA / don't-over-engineer constraints directly, calls out one real tradeoff, and ends decisively ('Given merchants are complaining, I'd go Redis'). Still longer than ideal but tightest of the three; no problem-restating preamble.

C.notes: Strong calibration — exploits the stated architecture context (Redis already in stack, monolith extraction) and gives a concrete ship order. Opinionated with a clear pick. Slightly verbose with code blocks and an A/B coupling sub-discussion; brief context-restating intro is a minor penalty.

analysis: All three are senior-level, opinionated, and correctly converge on a fast side-channel (Redis dirty-flag or client token) over write-through coupling or shorter TTL, addressing the EDA and throughput constraints. The differentiator is the user's preference for a concise, committed answer rather than an enumerated survey. B wins by being the tightest and most decisive: one recommendation, one tradeoff, a clear final call, minimal hedging. C is nearly as good and edges ahead on calibration by leveraging the given architecture context (Redis present, monolith), but it is longer with code and a coupling sub-debate. A is the weakest on style: technically excellent but the most verbose, presenting two full approaches and a dedicated 'avoid these' table, which reads as enumeration and runs well past the prompt length, contradicting the conciseness preference. None lands under 300 words, but B is closest to the proportional, do-X-not-here-are-7-options ideal.
